Figure~\ref{fig:action_r2_threecond} compares per-layer action probe $R^2$ across three training stages (untrained, Llama-2 base, VLA-trained) using 50 demonstrations per task and the same probe architecture.
All three conditions share L0 representations (the visual projector output), confirming that subsequent differences arise from Transformer processing rather than input variation.
The results suggest that VLA training performs layer-specific reorganization rather than uniform improvement.
At L1, trained action $R^2$ ($0.633$) is marginally lower than the pretrained LLM ($0.637$), consistent with the dual routing-encoding function of instruction-dominant heads (\S\ref{sec:learned_routing}): 24 heads integrate instruction access with action encoding at this layer.
In mid-layers (L2--L9), $R^2$ follows a consistent gradient (trained $>$ Llama-2 base $>$ untrained), with the trained peak shifting from L4 (Llama-2 base) to L8, consistent with deeper specialization for action-relevant feature integration.
In late layers (L21--L31), trained $R^2$ falls below the pretrained baseline (10 of 11 layers), suggesting these layers are repurposed for action token generation rather than state encoding.
The untrained model exhibits catastrophic negative $R^2$ at L10--L11, indicating that randomly initialized Transformer layers produce destructive interference on action-relevant structure.
This analysis uses a single seed without confidence intervals and should be interpreted as a supplementary observation.

To test the functional role of instruction-dominant heads, we ablate attention to instruction tokens at the readout position.
